chapters.title: Stack Structure
chapters.desc: A linear data structure governed by the Last-In, First-Out principle, providing a restricted access pattern for efficient memory management.
chapters.framework: A stack is a fundamental linear data structure that operates under the LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) architecture. It is characterized by a restricted access model where both additions (push) and removals (pop) occur at only one end, known as the 'top'. This single-ended interaction ensures that the most recently added element is always the first to be retrieved.
realWorldExamples: A stack of dinner plates: You add to the top and take from the top.
Browser History: The 'Back' button takes you to the most recently visited page.
The 'Undo' feature in software: It reverses the most recent action first.
A pile of books: The book placed last is the first to be picked up.

terminologies.def: Adding an element to the top of the stack.
Removing the top element from the stack.
Looking at the top element without removing it.
Checking if the stack has no elements.
Checking if the stack has reached its maximum capacity.

stackTypes.desc: Defined with a static size. memory is allocated at compile time. Risk of Overflow.
Grows and shrinks as needed. Memory is allocated at runtime. No size limit except physical RAM.

implementation: Select storage: Use an Array (Static) or Linked List (Dynamic).
Top Pointer: Set 'top' to -1 to represent an empty state.
Push Operation: Increment Top and store data at that position.
Pop Operation: Retrieve data at Top and decrement the pointer.
Underflow: Always check if Top == -1 before Popping.
Overflow: If using an Array, check if Top == MAX - 1 before Pushing.

chapters.title: Linked Lists
chapters.desc: Sequential access using node-based heap allocation.
chapters.framework: A linked list is a linear data structure, in which the elements are not stored at contiguous memory locations.
